summary: Develops a threat model for attacks on Internet confidentiality, written after the 2013 revelations of pervasive surveillance. It assumes an attacker who wants undetected, indiscriminate eavesdropping, and it is based on published, verified attacks. It is a problem statement and not a set of solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes ways a capable attacker could collect information from many Internet communications. It defines a threat model to help the Internet community understand the problem before designing mitigations.

questions: what is the threat model for pervasive surveillance
how do attackers eavesdrop on internet traffic
what is a passive pervasive attack
subtitle: A threat model for large-scale attacks that collect Internet communications without being noticed.

tldr.problem: The RFC describes threats to Internet confidentiality from attackers seeking broad, undetected access to communications.
tldr.mechanism: It defines an idealized passive attacker, adds capabilities illustrated by reported attacks, and classifies six ways to observe, infer, alter, or obtain communications.
tldr.outcome: This is a problem statement. Its Security Considerations section says mitigations are to be given in a future document.

facts.label: Idealized attacker
facts.value: Observes traffic and intermediate data at rest; does not modify communications

sections.title: Purpose and Key Terms
sections.content:
Following disclosures beginning in 2013, the RFC sets out to describe threats that exploit Internet communications for large-scale surveillance. Its focus is attacks that lead to undetected eavesdropping, rather than every possible attack.

A passive attack accesses a traffic flow without changing it; an active attack changes the flow. A pervasive attack uses access at many network points or otherwise obtains a large amount of traffic. Observation is taken directly from communications, while inference is derived by analyzing or correlating observations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives names to different ways an attacker can collect information. Listening to traffic is passive; changing traffic is active; inference means drawing conclusions from what was observed.

sections.title: The Idealized Passive Attacker
sections.content:
The idealized attacker can observe every packet on any network path and data at rest in intermediate systems. It can share information with other attackers but does not block, modify, or inject communications.

Encryption can prevent direct observation of content when implementations and keys are uncompromised. It does not hide all information: network and transport headers can expose addresses and ports, and traffic patterns can support inference.
sections.plainLanguage: Even when message contents are encrypted, a watcher may see which addresses communicate and when. The model starts with an attacker that observes broadly but does not alter traffic.

sections.title: How Observations Can Reveal Identity
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of correlating traffic with people. IP flow information can show which addresses communicate; reverse DNS or an ISP may link addresses to users; cleartext messaging logins, mail headers, or cookies can expose identity clues.

Graph analysis can associate addresses with similar use patterns. Link-layer identifiers such as MAC addresses and probed wireless network names can also help track devices and their owners.
sections.plainLanguage: Several clues can be connected to link traffic with a person. Addresses, login names, mail headers, cookies, and device identifiers can all contribute information.

sections.title: Reported Capabilities and Six Attack Classes
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes reports of large-scale collection, including cable access, access to service-provider data, decryption efforts, and active techniques that redirect or modify traffic. It uses those reports to expand the capabilities in its threat model.

The model has six classes: passive observation, passive inference, active attacks, static key exfiltration, dynamic key exfiltration, and content exfiltration. The last three involve a collaborator providing keys or data, either once, repeatedly, or from stored content.
sections.plainLanguage: The threat model includes listening, inferring, changing traffic, and obtaining keys or stored content through a participant. These methods have different costs and risks of discovery.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section states that this RFC describes a threat model for pervasive surveillance attacks. It says mitigations are to be provided in a future document.

The RFC therefore defines a problem space and attacker capabilities; it does not prescribe a set of technical countermeasures.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines the threat, not the defense. It leaves mitigations to a future document.
